question: I went to the testing center to take my final with extra time and they said they have no request from my professor. My exam is tomorrow. What can I do?

body.answer:
That's stressful, but one bad grade doesn't decide everything. Talking with your professor and an advisor soon can really help.

Contact your instructor right away: the faculty member is responsible for making sure alternative testing arrangements are provided [2]. Check your email or touch base with your instructor to make sure your exam accommodations are set up [3].

OSS says students must request an exam reservation through OSSOnline no later than ten business days in advance for final exams [2]. With the exam tomorrow, the usual deadline has passed. Contact the Alternative Testing staff at osstests@ramapo.edu (the best way to reach them) or your OSS counselor now to ask what can be arranged [4][5]. Faculty may also contact OSS at osstests@ramapo.edu [5].

**Office of Specialized Services**: Phone: (201) 684-7514. Email: oss@ramapo.edu. Location: C-Wing, Room 205. [25]

This office can help:
**Center for Student Success (Academic Advising)**: Phone: (201) 684-7441. Email: success@ramapo.edu. Office: D-207. [26]

Sources: [2](https://www.ramapo.edu/oss/what-faculty-need-to-know-about-students-with-disabilities/) [3](https://www.ramapo.edu/oss/alternative-testing-for-students/) [4](https://www.ramapo.edu/oss/alternative-testing-for-faculty/) [5](https://www.ramapo.edu/oss/alternative-testing-for-faculty/) [25](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/) [26](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

When a post-season game conflicts with a scheduled final exam/other culminating assessment, the student athlete must make arrangements with the instructor to reschedule the final exam/culminating assessment, as soon as the athletic contest schedule is known. (Note: Local conferences typically notify the College 24 to 48 hours in advance of the scheduled game.) Instructors are expected to accommodate such requests. When any issue arises, the Faculty Athletic Representative can serve as the intermediary and will be available to assist in making alternative arrangements (e.g., finding a proctor), if needed."}]}]}

question: I already have extra test time from the disability office but now I also need help with notes because I hurt my hand. How do I add that?

body.answer:
I'm sorry you're dealing with that, and I hope you feel better soon.

Contact the Office of Specialized Services (OSS) to discuss adding note-taking support. Accommodations are determined case-by-case; OSS encourages students seeking accommodations to contact its office [18]. For health impairments, potential accommodations include notetakers or scribes, audio-recording of classes, and electronic distribution of course materials [16].

**Office of Specialized Services**: Phone: (201) 684-7514. Email: oss@ramapo.edu. Location: C-Wing, Room 205. [30]

This office can help:
**Health Services**: Phone: (201) 684-7536. Location: Near the campus South Gate entrance at the corner of Route 202 and Hornbeam Road. [31]

Sources: [16](https://www.ramapo.edu/oss/disabilities-and-teaching-strategies-accommodations/) [18](https://www.ramapo.edu/oss/disabilities-and-teaching-strategies-accommodations/) [30](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/) [31](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

Examples of ways impairment may affect a student’s ability to participate include: Missing class for unpredictable and prolonged time periods Health problems may also interfere with the physical skills needed to complete laboratory, computer, or writing assignments Individuals with arthritis, for example, may have difficulty writing due to pain or joint deformities, making it a challenge for them to meet the writing requirements for some classes Students with Multiple Sclerosis may not be able to manipulate small laboratory equipment or complete tasks that require precise measuring, graphing, or drawing Prolonged sitting may pose challenges for an individual with chronic pain or back problems Illness or injury may result in limitations in mobility which require the need to use a wheelchair or scooter for mobility Some students must avoid specific activities that trigger their conditions. For example, a student with asthma may need to avoid specific inhalants in a lab. question: what laptop should i get for school, mac or windows?

body.answer:
**General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): Either can work well for school. Choose a Mac if you prefer macOS, have other Apple devices, and your coursework doesn’t require Windows-only software; choose Windows for broader software compatibility, more hardware choices, and often lower-cost options. Check your program’s software requirements first, then prioritize good battery life, a comfortable keyboard, and enough memory and storage for your needs.

Ramapo recommends:
- Business courses, including degree and certificate programs: choose a Windows computer, since many applications are only available for Windows. [1]
- Susan and Nick Vallario School of Arts, Humanities, and Education: you may want to consider a MacBook, as many applications for the program are Mac-based. [1]
- Other students: either Windows or Mac is sufficient. [1]
- Sciences, math, computer science, animation, video editing, and other computer-intensive fields: consider meeting or exceeding the recommended “High-end” specifications. [1]

Ramapo does not recommend a Chromebook currently, as it may not support the same applications as Windows and Mac laptops. [1]

MacBook recommendations: Minimum—MacBook Neo, MacOS 26 Tahoe or MacOS 27 Golden Gate, A18 Pro, 8 GB RAM, 256 GB SSD. Recommended—13” MacBook Air or 14″ MacBook Pro, MacOS 15 Sequoia, MacOS 26 Tahoe, or MacOS 27 Golden Gate, M3/M4 or higher, 16 GB or more RAM, 512GB SSD. High-end—14” MacBook Pro, MacOS 15 Sequoia, MacOS 26 Tahoe, or MacOS 27 Golden Gate, M5/M5 Pro or higher, 16 GB or more RAM, 1TB SSD. [2]

For Windows laptop specifications, see Ramapo’s [student laptop recommendations](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/). Questions? Contact the IT Help Desk. [1]

- **School of Arts, Humanities, and Education Office**: Phone: (201) 684-7365. Email: AHEOffice@ramapo.edu. Office: B-224. [33]
- **IT Help Desk**: Phone: (201) 684-7777. Email: helpdesk@ramapo.edu. Location: 4th floor of the Learning Commons. [33]

Sources: [1](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [2](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [33](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

answer:
**General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): Either can work well for school. Choose a Mac if you prefer macOS, have other Apple devices, and your coursework doesn’t require Windows-only software; choose Windows for broader software compatibility, more hardware choices, and often lower-cost options. Check your program’s software requirements first, then prioritize good battery life, a comfortable keyboard, and enough memory and storage for your needs.

Ramapo recommends:
- Business courses, including degree and certificate programs: choose a Windows computer, since many applications are only available for Windows. [1]
- Susan and Nick Vallario School of Arts, Humanities, and Education: you may want to consider a MacBook, as many applications for the program are Mac-based. [1]
- Other students: either Windows or Mac is sufficient. [1]
- Sciences, math, computer science, animation, video editing, and other computer-intensive fields: consider meeting or exceeding the recommended “High-end” specifications. [1]

Ramapo does not recommend a Chromebook currently, as it may not support the same applications as Windows and Mac laptops. [1]

MacBook recommendations: Minimum—MacBook Neo, MacOS 26 Tahoe or MacOS 27 Golden Gate, A18 Pro, 8 GB RAM, 256 GB SSD. Recommended—13” MacBook Air or 14″ MacBook Pro, MacOS 15 Sequoia, MacOS 26 Tahoe, or MacOS 27 Golden Gate, M3/M4 or higher, 16 GB or more RAM, 512GB SSD. High-end—14” MacBook Pro, MacOS 15 Sequoia, MacOS 26 Tahoe, or MacOS 27 Golden Gate, M5/M5 Pro or higher, 16 GB or more RAM, 1TB SSD. [2]

For Windows laptop specifications, see Ramapo’s [student laptop recommendations](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/). Questions? Contact the IT Help Desk. [1]

- **School of Arts, Humanities, and Education Office**: Phone: (201) 684-7365. Email: AHEOffice@ramapo.edu. Office: B-224. [33]
- **IT Help Desk**: Phone: (201) 684-7777. Email: helpdesk@ramapo.edu. Location: 4th floor of the Learning Commons. [33]

Sources: [1](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [2](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [33](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

question: is it better to take 15 or 18 credits first semester

body.answer:
I can't choose for you, but I can share what the college publishes.

Ramapo says most students take 4 courses a semester, averaging 16 credits, and that taking 16 credits each semester for eight semesters allows students to meet the 128-credit graduation requirement. Tuition and tuition-related fees are a flat rate between 12 and 18 credits. [1]

Its first-semester guidance says first-year students are placed into four courses based on their declared major (or general education courses if undeclared), and should focus on doing well academically and getting involved. [9] So its published guidance doesn’t specifically recommend 15 rather than 18 credits; it describes a typical load of 16 credits. [1]

First-year students are assigned professional advisors in the Center for Student Success. [14] Students meet an advisor during the In Person Advisement session; follow the steps in your Admissions portal ([http://apply.ramapo.edu/status](http://apply.ramapo.edu/status)) for specific information. Federal regulations set forth that the amount of student work typically required to meet the stated learning outcomes of a course, learning experience, or competency approximates one hour of instruction or examination and two hours of student preparation every week across a fifteen-week semester for every credit hour that the student is awarded.
The guidelines of the Middle States Commission on Higher Education provide conventional calculations for specific course types. Those calculations are reflected below.
A clock hour consists of 60 minutes, while a credit hour consists of 50 minutes. The calculations below are based on a 60-minute clock hour.
A face-to-face 4-credit lecture- or seminar-based undergraduate course typically meets the following criteria:
A minimum of 15 weeks of instruction or examination per semester. If the course includes a final exam, the final exam will take place during week 15. If the course does not include a final exam, week 15 should be devoted to instruction or some other organized learning activity.
A minimum of one day of instruction per week;
A minimum of 200 minutes of classroom instruction or examination per week;
A minimum of 400 minutes of out-of-class student preparation per week.
All other four-credit undergraduate courses should meet the following criteria or their approximate equivalents:
Online courses:
A minimum of 200 minutes of (online) instruction, examination, discussion, tutorial, or other appropriate learning activity, and;
A minimum of 400 minutes of out-of-class student work per week across 15 weeks.
Studio courses:
A minimum of 600 minutes of supervised and/or independent practice.
Internships, co-ops, clinicals, field work, supervised teaching, and independent studies:
A minimum of 600 minutes of supervised and/or independent practice and/or work per week across 15 weeks. A portion of this time may be used for classroom instruction and/or out-of-class student preparation.
Undergraduate courses are generally offered with 4 credits. Undergraduate courses bearing fewer than four credits (other than laboratory courses) adjust their meeting and preparation times proportionately in accordance with the criteria for 4-credit courses. For example, a one-credit undergraduate course should meet the following criteria:
A minimum of 50 minutes a week for classroom instruction or examination, and;
A minimum of 100 minutes of out-of-class student preparation per week across a 15-week semester.
Undergraduate laboratory courses may vary in credit but always meet the following criteria:
A minimum of 150 minutes a week for lecture, discussion, and/or laboratory work, and;
A minimum of 100 minutes of out-of-class student work per week across a 15-week semester for every student credit hour assigned.

answer:
I can't choose for you, but I can share what the college publishes.

Ramapo says most students take 4 courses a semester, averaging 16 credits, and that taking 16 credits each semester for eight semesters allows students to meet the 128-credit graduation requirement. Tuition and tuition-related fees are a flat rate between 12 and 18 credits. [1]

Its first-semester guidance says first-year students are placed into four courses based on their declared major (or general education courses if undeclared), and should focus on doing well academically and getting involved. [9] So its published guidance doesn’t specifically recommend 15 rather than 18 credits; it describes a typical load of 16 credits. [1]

First-year students are assigned professional advisors in the Center for Student Success. [14] Students meet an advisor during the In Person Advisement session; follow the steps in your Admissions portal ([http://apply.ramapo.edu/status](http://apply.ramapo.edu/status)) for specific information. [5]

- **Center for Student Success (Academic Advising)**: Phone: (201) 684-7441. Email: success@ramapo.edu. Office: D-207. [35]
- **Admissions**: Phone: (201) 684-7300. Email: admissions@ramapo.edu. Location: McBride House. [35]

question: Is there a club for international students, or for Indian students?

body.answer:
Yes. The International Student Organization (ISO) seeks students of all nationalities and plans activities and events for members and the Ramapo community. Its activities include international dinner nights, films, lectures, off-campus trips, and International Student Week. Contact ISO at iso@ramapo.edu. [21]

For Indian or South Asian students, South Asian Club brings South Asians together and raises awareness of South Asian culture; it welcomes anyone interested. Contact southasians@ramapo.edu. [24][3]

NAACH is an inclusive South Asian dance club open to anyone interested, including Bollywood, Nepali folk dance, and South Asian classical styles. Contact naach@ramapo.edu. [26]

**Center for Student Involvement**: Phone: (201) 684-7593. Email: csi@ramapo.edu. Office: SC-202. [58]

Making friends with international students was especially positive because they brought cultural perspectives I likely wouldn’t have been exposed to had I not had international classmates. Befriending and having genuine conversations with students of diverse nationalities taught me important things about other parts of the world that I couldn’t have learned from a book or movie or anywhere else. The fact that these students and I attended the same classes and shared the common experience of being a Ramapo student made all the difference in what we were able to share with and teach each other. I have many great memories of the times I spent with my international friends, and my Ramapo experience would not have been the same without those friendships. —Laura French, Ramapo College Class of 2016 Alt Break trip to New Mexico At Ramapo College of New Jersey, I majored in International Studies (https://www.ramapo.edu/ahe/convening-group-international-studies/). The presence of international students on campus, along with the college’s focus on incorporating international perspectives, greatly enhanced my overall college experience. While I never got to study abroad, the on-campus activities, curriculum, professors and most importantly, the international students, at Ramapo College taught me to reach for goals at global scale, and encouraged me to be curious and open to new cultures. It allowed me to become a better global citizen. —Brianne Kennedy, Ramapo College Class of 2015 I graduated Ramapo College in 2013. My time at school was largely impacted by international education as a whole, and by extension the international student population. I specifically remember a Global Roadrunners (https://www.ramapo.edu/study-abroad/roadrunners/) organized outing where study abroad alumni and international students grabbed lunch at a Dim Sum restaurant. The international students graciously helped us with ordering and provided explanations for all the different dishes we tried. It was my first time trying Dim Sum, but it certainly wasn’t my last (the next time – I was actually in Hong Kong!) I can certainly say that my time at Ramapo College was enriched by our international student community and influenced many of my future life decisions. question: how many credits do i still need for my major

body.answer:
I can't see your personal records, like your grades, balance, schedule or financial aid status.

To check how many credits you still need for your major, view your degree evaluation. It outlines your class requirements for your major. [12]

1. Visit [https://web.ramapo.edu/](https://web.ramapo.edu/) [12]
2. Click on Web for Students. [12]
3. Click on Web Registration. [12]
4. Enter the Secure Area and type in your Ramapo login and password. [12]
5. Click on Student and Financial Aid, then Student Records, then Degree Evaluation. [12]
6. Select the current term and click enter. Click Generate New Evaluation. [12]
7. Click the circle next to your major and click Generate Request. Select detail requirements and click Submit. [12]

I can’t determine how many credits you personally still need from the information provided. Review your degree audit and meet with your adviser to ensure you have met all requirements for graduation. [1]

**Financial Aid**: Phone: (201) 684-7549. Email: finaid@ramapo.edu. Office: E-210. [34]

Sources: [1](https://www.ramapo.edu/registrar/faq/) [12](https://www.ramapo.edu/studentsuccess/faq/) [34](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

Recognizing that the college is creating a limited public forum, the college retains the right to limit access, and postings, to college systems. As a means to foster intellectual pursuits, the college will make every effort to respect the privacy of all users. However, for technical reasons related to system architecture and maintenance needs, privacy cannot be guaranteed at all times and users must take this into account when composing email or surfing the Web. An expectation of privacy is further limited by the needs of the college to comply with State and Federal laws, protect the rights of students, faculty, staff, board members, and invitees, and/or to meet administrative objectives. Ramapo College faculty and staff are provided with e-mail accounts for the purpose of conducting official college business related to instructional, academic and/or administrative activities to accomplish tasks consistent with the college’s mission. Because email is an effective way to disseminate information of importance, relevance and interest, and because it is an important tool to meet the academic and administrative needs of the college community, it shall be the college’s policy that electronic mail (email) be an official communication mechanism with faculty, staff, and students and that all faculty, staff, and students are required to maintain an “@ramapo.edu” address. This is the only email address that will be used for official communication with faculty, staff, and students regarding all academic and administrative matters. Retired tenured faculty and retired staff with at least ten years of service may be permitted to retain their e-mail accounts upon request. question: is it worth getting a masters right after graduating or should i work first

body.answer:
**General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): It depends on the field and your goals. A master’s right away can make sense if it’s required for your career, you’re sure about your specialization, or funding is strong. Working first can help you test what you enjoy, build experience, and choose a program with clearer purpose—some employers may also help pay for it. Compare likely career benefits with tuition, lost earnings, and the value of gaining experience.

Ramapo describes both paths, but does not say one is best for everyone. Its 4+1 option says a master’s can mean greater opportunities for higher salaries and higher-level positions, take one year after undergraduate rather than two, save about $11,000 or 30% of the total master’s degree cost, and still allow students to enter the workforce right after undergraduate graduation. Graduate courses are in the evening, ideal for working professionals. [7]

For the work-first path, Ramapo says job experience matters: “majors don’t get you a job. Job experience does.” It recommends co-op or internship experience before graduating. [21] Its career guidance also suggests sharing your job-search strategy with your Career Advisor, while senior-year students are advised to finalize and send graduate school applications by deadlines. [33]

To help decide, speak with your advisor as soon as possible to create a personal calendar if considering graduate school. [30] Ramapo also encourages meeting with a professor to discuss graduate school; Professor Barnes would be happy to discuss PhD programs with interested students: toddbarnes@ramapo.edu. [3] The Cahill Career Development Center is another place to seek help; its decision-making guidance recommends its computer tests to help recognize your abilities. [21]

**Cahill Career Development Center**: Phone: Main Office (201) 684-7444; ASB Office (201) 684-7675. Email: careercenter@ramapo.edu. Main Office: C-209; ASB Office: ASB-513. [36]

Sources: [3](https://www.ramapo.edu/ahe/convening-group-webs/english-literary-studies-major/career-opportunities/grad-school/) [7](https://www.ramapo.edu/dmc/4plus1/) [21](https://www.ramapo.edu/studentsuccess/major/) [30](https://www.ramapo.edu/sssw/psychology/faqs/) [33](https://www.ramapo.edu/careercenter/four-year-plan/) [36](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

answer:
**General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): It depends on the field and your goals. A master’s right away can make sense if it’s required for your career, you’re sure about your specialization, or funding is strong. Working first can help you test what you enjoy, build experience, and choose a program with clearer purpose—some employers may also help pay for it. Compare likely career benefits with tuition, lost earnings, and the value of gaining experience.

Ramapo describes both paths, but does not say one is best for everyone. Its 4+1 option says a master’s can mean greater opportunities for higher salaries and higher-level positions, take one year after undergraduate rather than two, save about $11,000 or 30% of the total master’s degree cost, and still allow students to enter the workforce right after undergraduate graduation. Graduate courses are in the evening, ideal for working professionals. [7]

For the work-first path, Ramapo says job experience matters: “majors don’t get you a job. Job experience does.” It recommends co-op or internship experience before graduating. [21] Its career guidance also suggests sharing your job-search strategy with your Career Advisor, while senior-year students are advised to finalize and send graduate school applications by deadlines. [33]

To help decide, speak with your advisor as soon as possible to create a personal calendar if considering graduate school. [30] Ramapo also encourages meeting with a professor to discuss graduate school; Professor Barnes would be happy to discuss PhD programs with interested students: toddbarnes@ramapo.edu. [3] The Cahill Career Development Center is another place to seek help; its decision-making guidance recommends its computer tests to help recognize your abilities. [21]

**Cahill Career Development Center**: Phone: Main Office (201) 684-7444; ASB Office (201) 684-7675. Email: careercenter@ramapo.edu. Main Office: C-209; ASB Office: ASB-513. [36]

question: Which clubs do you recommend to meet American students?

body.answer:
**General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): Try joining student clubs, study groups, sports, or campus events, and start conversations before or after class. You can also connect through shared-interest groups or language exchanges. Be friendly, ask about their interests, and suggest a casual coffee or study session if the conversation goes well.

Ramapo says all clubs are open to all students, and joining can provide interesting friends. [6] For meeting students across backgrounds, I’d suggest the International Student Organization: it seeks students of all nationalities to create intercultural experiences and holds activities for members and the wider Ramapo community. [9] Culture Club’s mission is to bring people together by sharing each other’s culture. [34] Ramapo’s culturally based organizations also welcome students who want to learn and connect; examples include the Black Student Union, Students of Caribbean Ancestry, Filipino American Student Association, and United Asian Association. [31]

If you mean specifically American students, Ramapo does not identify clubs as a way to meet American students, so I don’t have verified information about which clubs are best for that. The American Marketing Association is open to all majors and offers networking events. [https://www.ramapo.edu/clubs/organization/american-marketing-association-ama/](https://www.ramapo.edu/clubs/organization/american-marketing-association-ama/) [12]

**Center for Student Involvement**: Phone: (201) 684-7593. Email: csi@ramapo.edu. Office: SC-202. [58]

Sources: [6](https://www.ramapo.edu/clubs/) [9](https://www.ramapo.edu/clubs/organization/international-student-organization-iso/) [12](https://www.ramapo.edu/clubs/organization/american-marketing-association-ama/) [31](https://www.ramapo.edu/oabc/home/you-belong-at-ramapo/) [34](https://archway.ramapo.edu/CultClub/) [58](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

answer:
**General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): Try joining student clubs, study groups, sports, or campus events, and start conversations before or after class. You can also connect through shared-interest groups or language exchanges. Be friendly, ask about their interests, and suggest a casual coffee or study session if the conversation goes well.

Ramapo says all clubs are open to all students, and joining can provide interesting friends. [6] For meeting students across backgrounds, I’d suggest the International Student Organization: it seeks students of all nationalities to create intercultural experiences and holds activities for members and the wider Ramapo community. [9] Culture Club’s mission is to bring people together by sharing each other’s culture. [34] Ramapo’s culturally based organizations also welcome students who want to learn and connect; examples include the Black Student Union, Students of Caribbean Ancestry, Filipino American Student Association, and United Asian Association. [31]

If you mean specifically American students, Ramapo does not identify clubs as a way to meet American students, so I don’t have verified information about which clubs are best for that. The American Marketing Association is open to all majors and offers networking events. [https://www.ramapo.edu/clubs/organization/american-marketing-association-ama/](https://www.ramapo.edu/clubs/organization/american-marketing-association-ama/) [12]

**Center for Student Involvement**: Phone: (201) 684-7593. Email: csi@ramapo.edu. Office: SC-202. [58]

general.asked: How can I meet American students?
general.text: Try joining student clubs, study groups, sports, or campus events, and start conversations before or after class. You can also connect through shared-interest groups or language exchanges. Be friendly, ask about their interests, and suggest a casual coffee or study session if the conversation goes well.

question: which is better here, the MBA or the masters in accounting

body.answer:
I can't choose for you, but I can share what the college publishes.

There isn’t a published answer to which is “better”; the choice depends on your goals. Ramapo describes its MBA as preparing students for leadership across commercial enterprises and nonprofits, with a global business foundation, ethical leadership and skills in data-informed decisions [2]. It offers 30- or 42-credit options, online/hybrid format, full- or part-time study, and a 1-year full-time or 2-year part-time duration. The listed cost is $1,318.65 per credit; $39,559.50 for 30 credits or $55,383.30 for 42 credits [4]. The MBA page offers “Schedule an Advisor Session with the MBA Director” [4].

Ramapo describes its MS in Accounting (MSAC) as for those seeking CPA certification or advanced accounting knowledge. It says the program covers 150 credits required for the CPA license and is aligned with New Jersey State Board of Accountancy requirements [5]. The program is 30 credits, hybrid/online, full- or part-time, with 1-year full-time or 2-year part-time duration. Listed cost is $1,091.10 per credit, or $32,733.00 total [8]. It offers “Schedule a MS in Accounting Advisor Session”; the director’s message says students receive academic and career guidance and advisement [9].

The Anisfield School of Business says it provides academic advisement, career guidance and professional development, with faculty mentoring and one-on-one engagement [12]. Contact the Anisfield School of Business to ask for guidance comparing programs.

- **Ramapo College Foundation**: Phone: (201) 684-6819. Institutional Advancement: Birch Mansion. [16]
- **Anisfield School of Business**: Phone: Phone (201) 684-7379; Phone (201) 684-7380; Phone (201) 684-7378; Fax (201) 684-7957. Email: asb@ramapo.edu. Office: ASB-333. [16]

Sources: [2](https://catalog.ramapo.edu/programs/SB-MBA-MBAD) [4](https://www.ramapo.edu/mba/) [5](https://www.ramapo.edu/msac/) [8](https://www.ramapo.edu/msac/) [9](https://www.ramapo.edu/msac/) [12](https://www.ramapo.edu/asb/about/) [16](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

answer:
I can't choose for you, but I can share what the college publishes.

There isn’t a published answer to which is “better”; the choice depends on your goals. Ramapo describes its MBA as preparing students for leadership across commercial enterprises and nonprofits, with a global business foundation, ethical leadership and skills in data-informed decisions [2]. It offers 30- or 42-credit options, online/hybrid format, full- or part-time study, and a 1-year full-time or 2-year part-time duration. The listed cost is $1,318.65 per credit; $39,559.50 for 30 credits or $55,383.30 for 42 credits [4]. The MBA page offers “Schedule an Advisor Session with the MBA Director” [4].

Ramapo describes its MS in Accounting (MSAC) as for those seeking CPA certification or advanced accounting knowledge. It says the program covers 150 credits required for the CPA license and is aligned with New Jersey State Board of Accountancy requirements [5]. The program is 30 credits, hybrid/online, full- or part-time, with 1-year full-time or 2-year part-time duration. Listed cost is $1,091.10 per credit, or $32,733.00 total [8]. It offers “Schedule a MS in Accounting Advisor Session”; the director’s message says students receive academic and career guidance and advisement [9].

The Anisfield School of Business says it provides academic advisement, career guidance and professional development, with faculty mentoring and one-on-one engagement [12]. Contact the Anisfield School of Business to ask for guidance comparing programs.

- **Ramapo College Foundation**: Phone: (201) 684-6819. Institutional Advancement: Birch Mansion. [16]
- **Anisfield School of Business**: Phone: Phone (201) 684-7379; Phone (201) 684-7380; Phone (201) 684-7378; Fax (201) 684-7957. Email: asb@ramapo.edu. Office: ASB-333. [16]

Direct deposit is also known as Electronic Funds Transfer (EFT). It is the transfer of funds from Ramapo College to an individual student’s checking or savings account at a participating bank, savings and loan association or credit union. Direct deposit delivers your money quickly and safely. The difference is a check isn’t printed or mailed. Are there any costs for my participating in Direct Deposit? No, the program is offered as a service to our students. I’m interested in Direct Deposit, but I do not know if it is for me? If you have an account, visit your bank or credit union. They can answer your questions about Direct Deposit. If you do not have an account, consider opening one. Many banks offer a variety of accounts, some with little or no fees. Where do I sign up for Direct Deposit? Click here for instructions (https://www.ramapo.edu/student-accounts/direct-deposit/). The Payment Profile asks for my checking or saving account number and my bank’s transit routing number. How do I find that information? Checking and savings account numbers are normally noted at the bottom of checks and deposit slips as well as the nine digit bank transit routing number. If you need assistance, come to the Office of Student Accounts, first floor, D-Wing. When I sign up for Direct Deposit, how long does it take before my money is available in my account? When you sign up for Direct Deposit, you can expect your refund to be deposited into your account within one to two weeks of the application being submitted. This pertains only to students that are eligible for a refund because of either overpayment by a loan or financial aid or for students that drop classes within the appropriate add/drop dates. When can I use my money? Your money is available for use as soon as it is deposited into your account. You can write checks, withdraw money and transfer into different accounts. Anything you usually do with your money now, you can also do with Direct Deposit. After I sign up for Direct Deposit, do I have to stay with the same bank? No, you can use Direct Deposit at any bank.
